q.q: In human–computer interaction, what is meant by the user interface?
o: The set of device drivers that let the operating system send output to the screen and read the keyboard
The part of the operating system that loads programs and allocates memory and processor time to them
Everything through which a person and a computer exchange information, including what is shown and how commands are given
The colour scheme, fonts, icons and graphical theme that a designer chooses for the windows of one particular application
q.why: The user interface covers all the ways information passes between the user and the computer: displays, sound, keyboard, mouse, touch and voice.

q.q: What is the main aim of human–computer interaction (HCI) design?
o: To make systems use as little memory and processing power as possible
To make systems effective, efficient and satisfying for the people who actually use them
To make programs portable so they run on any operating system
To make interfaces look modern and professional by following the latest trends in visual design
q.why: HCI focuses on the people using the system; low resource use or a modern look are not its main aim.

q.q: A file-upload page shows a progress bar and a percentage while the file is sent. Which feature of a good interface does this mainly show?
o: Responsive
Forgiving
Simple
Attractive
q.why: A responsive interface keeps up with the user and always shows its current status; the progress bar is feedback on what the system is doing.

q.q: A photo app asks 'Are you sure you want to delete?' and moves deleted photos to a recycle bin. Which feature of a good interface is this?
o: Responsive
Intuitive and consistent
Simple
Forgiving
q.why: A forgiving interface makes mistakes easy to reverse. A confirmation prompt is not feedback on status, so 'responsive' is the wrong choice.

q.q: In every screen of an app the 'Save' command is in the same place with the same icon. Which feature of a good interface is this?
o: Simple
Forgiving
Intuitive and consistent
Responsive
q.why: Controls that behave the same way throughout let knowledge transfer from one screen to the next.

q.q: Why can a slow interface that gives no feedback lead to a customer paying twice?
o: The customer thinks the software has crashed and presses the pay button again
The interface is unforgiving, so it has no way of reversing the first payment
Inconsistent button positions make the customer press the wrong button
The form does not validate the amount before the payment is submitted
q.why: Without feedback the user cannot tell the system is working, so they repeat the action. The other options describe different problems.

q.q: Which answer would earn credit for describing a feature of a good user interface?
o: Easy to use, so that users can work with it without any problems at all
User friendly, so that everyone is able to use the system really easily
Nice to look at, so that users like using the software a lot more
Consistent layout, so what users learn on one screen transfers to the others
q.why: 'Easy to use' or 'user friendly' on its own is too vague; a good answer names the feature and says what it means or why it helps.

q.q: What does WIMP stand for?
o: Windows, icons, mouse, pointer
Windows, icons, menus, pointer
Windows, icons, menus, programs
Workspaces, icons, menus, pointer
q.why: The four elements are windows, icons, menus and pointer. 'Mouse' is not the M; the pointer is the P.

q.q: In a WIMP interface, what are 'windows'?
o: Versions of the Microsoft operating system that provide a graphical interface
Rectangular areas of the screen in which applications or documents run
Lists of options to choose from, such as drop-down menus or a ribbon
Small pictures that represent programs, files, folders or devices
q.why: Windows means screen windows, several of which can be open at once, not the Microsoft product.

q.q: In Windows, what does the command dir /s do that dir on its own does not?
o: Lists the files in the current folder and in all its subfolders
Lists only the system files that are in the current folder
Sorts the files in the current folder into order of size
Lists the files in the current folder one screen at a time
q.why: The /s switch extends the listing to every subfolder; dir alone lists only the current folder.

q.q: In the command ipconfig /all, what name is given to the /all part that modifies the command?
o: A script
A prompt
A parameter file
A switch
q.why: Switches are extra parameters that change what a command does. A script is a saved sequence of commands.

q.q: Why do new users usually find a graphical interface easier than a command line?
o: Commands are typed in plain English, so users do not need to learn exact syntax
Sequences of actions are saved as scripts and replayed automatically for them
Options are shown on screen so users recognise them rather than having to recall them
It needs less memory and processing, so it responds faster on any computer
q.why: In a GUI, users recognise icons and menu options instead of remembering commands. GUIs actually need more resources, not fewer.

q.q: Why can a forms dialogue interface validate data as it is entered?
o: Each field is a separate control, so each entry can be checked as it is completed
The user types commands with exact syntax, so mistakes are rejected at the prompt
The pointer can only select options that appear in the drop-down menus
The whole form is sent to the server, which checks every field at the end
q.why: Because each text box, list or check box is its own control, its value can be checked immediately.

q.q: Which statement about a menu-driven interface is correct?
o: It is the M in WIMP and means exactly the same as a drop-down menu in a GUI
It is a series of option screens, as on a kiosk, and is not the same as the menus inside a GUI
It requires the user to type commands chosen from a printed menu, each one with its own exact syntax
It is another name for a forms dialogue that uses radio buttons and text boxes
q.why: The notes warn that a menu-driven interface (screens of limited options) differs from the menus within a WIMP interface.

q.q: Compared with a command line, which is a disadvantage of a WIMP interface?
o: It is harder for beginners because commands must be recalled
It cannot move data between applications by copy and paste
It offers no keyboard shortcuts for experienced users
It needs more RAM, storage and processing power and a good display
q.why: Graphics need more hardware resources. The other options are actually strengths of a GUI or untrue.

q.q: A network technician must create 400 new pupil accounts at the start of term. Which interface is most suitable, and why?
o: WIMP, because icons and menus make each individual account quick to set up
Forms dialogue, because each account's fields are validated as they are typed
Command line, because a script can repeat the command for every pupil in seconds
Menu-driven, because the limited choices on each screen mean fewer errors
q.why: An expert doing a repetitive technical job benefits most from scripting at the command line.

q.q: A parent wants to book a swimming session at a leisure centre online. Which interface is most suitable?
o: Command line, as it is the fastest interface for any type of user
WIMP, as a WYSIWYG preview lets the parent see the final booking
Natural language, as the parent may type the booking in any words
Forms dialogue, as the guided, validated fields need no training
q.why: Public data collection suits forms: no commands to learn and the limited options are exactly what is needed.

q.q: A pupil is designing a poster for the school show. Which interface suits this task best?
o: WIMP, for visual layout, drag and drop and a WYSIWYG preview
Command line, because commands give precise control of every pixel
Forms dialogue, because each part of the poster is a validated field
Menu-driven, because a few fixed options make design quicker
q.why: Visual design benefits from a graphical interface, and a normal PC meets its hardware demands.

q.q: Why is the risk of a serious error higher with a command line than with a GUI?
o: Command lines use more RAM, so the computer crashes more often
Each command is validated as it is typed, which often blocks perfectly correct input
One mistyped command may fail or even delete data, with few clues or confirmations
The pointer can easily click the wrong icon and start a program
q.why: GUIs typically give confirmations and undo; at a prompt a typo is executed exactly as typed.

q.q: An experienced clerk enters hundreds of orders a day through a forms dialogue interface and finds it frustrating. What is the most likely reason?
o: Forms need a powerful processor and a high-resolution display
Moving through every field in turn is tedious for experienced users
Forms cannot validate data, so mistakes must be fixed afterwards
Every command has to be memorised and typed with exact syntax
q.why: Forms are easy for beginners but slow and restrictive for experts. They need little processing and do validate input.

q.q: Which is the best justification for an advanced programmer preferring a command line?
o: It is easier to learn because options are recognised on screen rather than recalled
It prevents serious errors by asking for confirmation before every action is carried out
Knowing the commands makes it the fastest interface, and repetitive jobs can be scripted
It shows a WYSIWYG preview of the result before each command is actually run
q.why: Speed comes from already knowing the commands; scripting and low resource use are the other credited points.

q.q: A teacher wants to turn a printed worksheet into editable text on a desktop PC. Which method should be used?
o: Photograph it with a webcam and save it as a JPEG
Scan it and use optical mark recognition (OMR)
Scan it and save the result as a bitmap image
Scan it and use optical character recognition (OCR)
q.why: OCR recognises the characters in the scanned image and turns them into text; a plain image or OMR does not.

q.q: In speech recognition, what happens immediately after the microphone captures the user's voice?
o: Software matches the sounds against known words
An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) digitises the sound
The recognised words are displayed as text on the screen straight away
The sound is compressed into MP3 format for storage
q.why: The order is: microphone captures sound, ADC digitises it, then software matches sounds to words.

q.q: Which smartphone user would benefit most from speech recognition for entering text?
o: A user with limited mobility who finds typing on a small keyboard difficult
A user sending a message from a noisy building site
A user typing a password on a crowded train
A user who wants to dictate a private message while sitting in a quiet meeting
q.why: Speech-to-text helps users with dyslexia or limited mobility; noise and privacy are disadvantages of voice input.

q.q: Why do on-screen smartphone keyboards use predictive text?
o: To check spelling against a dictionary after the message is sent
To compress the message so it uses less mobile data
To reduce typing on a small screen by suggesting whole words
To convert stylus strokes into characters as they are drawn
q.why: Predictive text speeds up entry on small touch keyboards by offering whole words.

q.q: How does handwriting recognition on a tablet work?
o: An image of the screen is scanned and OCR is applied to the picture
The path of the stylus is analysed and matched to letters, then stored as text
The stylus records the sound of the writing, which is then converted into words
Each tap of the stylus sends a character code just like a key press
q.why: The stylus path is analysed and matched to letters; OCR works on scanned printed pages instead.

q.q: Why does a smartphone compress video, for example to MP4, as it records?
o: To make the recording lossless so no detail is lost
To increase the resolution of each recorded frame
To remove background noise from the soundtrack
To reduce the file size so it can be stored and shared
q.why: Uncompressed video would fill storage very quickly; compression makes storing and sharing practical.

q.q: Why might a podcaster record on a desktop PC rather than a smartphone?
o: A high-quality external microphone can be used, picking up less background noise
Desktops compress the audio on the device as it is recorded, so the files are much smaller
Smartphones cannot record sound for longer than a few minutes
Desktop microphones convert the sound directly into text
q.why: Desktops can use high-quality external microphones; built-in phone mics are convenient but pick up more background noise.

q.q: A railway ticket machine shows 'Single', 'Return', 'Season ticket' and 'Help' on each screen. Which type of interface is this?
o: Forms dialogue
Natural language
Command line
Menu-driven
q.why: The user chooses from a limited list of options at each level, which is a menu-driven interface.

q.q: A voice assistant writes 'their' when the user said 'there'. Which weakness of voice interfaces does this show?
o: Homophones sound the same, so recognition can pick the wrong word
Voice interfaces need a separate training session for every word
The microphone samples too slowly to capture short words
Voice commands must follow an exact syntax to be accepted
q.why: Homophones such as there/their are a known source of recognition errors, along with noise and accents.

q.q: Which is a particular concern with biometric interfaces?
o: Users may forget or lose their biometric characteristic
Storing biometric data raises security and ethical concerns
Other people can easily forge the characteristic
A keyboard is needed to confirm the user's identity
q.why: Biometric data is sensitive and cannot be changed if stolen. It cannot be forgotten and is hard to forge.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a touch-sensitive interface?
o: Gestures must be learned as exact commands and typed in full
A separate keyboard and mouse are always needed alongside it, which takes up more desk space
Small targets are hard to select, and screens get dirty, scratched or broken
Background noise and accents stop gestures being recognised
q.why: Touch is intuitive and saves space, but small targets and screen damage or dirt are its drawbacks.

q.q: A user types 'show me trains to Derry next Friday' and is given times for the wrong week. Which weakness of a natural language interface does this show?
o: Commands must be typed with exact syntax and switches
Only the options provided on each screen can be chosen
Everyday language is ambiguous and can be misinterpreted
The interface must be trained to the user's accent
q.why: Natural language interfaces need no commands but can misread ambiguous requests such as 'next Friday'.

q.q: Why is a voice interface a poor choice for patients checking in at a busy GP surgery?
o: Patients would have to remember a set of commands with exact syntax
The waiting room is noisy and patients may not want to say personal details aloud
Voice interfaces cannot help those patients who are unable to read the words shown on the screen
Voice systems need large on-screen buttons that must be cleaned often
q.why: Background noise causes misrecognition and speaking aloud raises privacy issues; voice actually helps those who cannot read the screen.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a biometric interface?
o: The characteristic is unique to the person and cannot be forgotten or lost
The stored data can easily be changed by the user if it is ever stolen by a hacker
The scanners are cheap to buy and simple to install
Physical features never change with age or illness
q.why: Biometrics are unique, unforgettable and hard to forge, but they are expensive and some features change over time.

q.q: Showing all the options on screen, rather than expecting users to remember commands, follows which HCI principle?
o: Feedback
Consistency
Error prevention and recovery
Minimise memory load
q.why: Users recognise options rather than recall them, which minimises memory load.

q.q: Which design features mainly help users with a hearing impairment?
o: Alt text, high contrast and resizable text
Captions, transcripts and visual alerts
Keyboard navigation and large touch targets
Plain language and one task per screen
q.why: Captions and transcripts present spoken content as text, and visual alerts replace sounds.

q.q: Which design features mainly help users with a motor impairment?
o: Full keyboard navigation, large targets and no tight time limits
Captions and subtitles on every video clip shown on the site
Alternative text for images and resizable text
Plain language and a clear, consistent structure
q.why: Motor impairments make precise mouse use and fast responses difficult, so keyboard access, big targets and time matter.

q.q: A form marks required fields only by colouring their labels red. Why is this poor design?
o: Red text cannot be read aloud by any screen reader
Coloured labels use more memory and slow the page down
Red is reserved only for error messages under the accessibility guidelines for websites
Users with colour blindness may not be able to tell which fields are required
q.why: Colour should never be the only cue; adding the word 'required' fixes it.

q.q: Which is an example of the 'error prevention and recovery' principle?
o: Keeping the same colours and terminology on every screen
Showing a progress bar during a long upload
Asking for confirmation before a file is permanently deleted
Using large buttons because users wear gloves
q.why: Confirming destructive actions, validating input and offering undo all prevent or recover from errors.

q.q: A factory touch screen is given large buttons because workers wear thick gloves. Which HCI principle is being applied?
o: Feedback
Suit the user
Minimise memory load
Consistency
q.why: Suiting the user means considering their environment, including noise, light and gloves.

q.q: In Northern Ireland, which law places a duty on service providers to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, including for online services?
o: Equality Act 2010 and its regulations
Data Protection Act 2018
Disability Discrimination Act 1995 (as amended)
Computer Misuse Act 1990
q.why: In NI the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 applies; the Equality Act 2010 covers Great Britain.

q.q: What is data compression?
o: Encrypting data so that it occupies less space on the disk
Lowering the colour depth or sample rate of every file
Moving data onto a physically smaller storage device
Encoding data using fewer bits than the original representation
q.why: Compression re-encodes data in fewer bits, usually by removing redundancy.

q.q: Why can most files be compressed?
o: They contain redundancy, such as repeated words or areas of the same colour
They contain parity bits that can safely be removed
They are stored in denary, which takes up much more space than the same data in binary
They contain metadata that is never used by any program
q.why: Repeated or predictable data can be stored more efficiently; that redundancy is what compression removes.

q.q: Mark schemes credit two reasons for compressing files. Which pair is correct?
o: To reduce storage space, and to improve the quality of the file
To improve security, and to reduce transmission time
To reduce storage space, and to reduce transmission time
To reduce processing time, and to reduce storage space
q.why: Compression saves storage and speeds up upload, download and streaming. It costs processing time rather than saving it.

q.q: Which is a cost of using compression?
o: Processing time is needed to compress and decompress the data
Compressed files always take longer to download than originals
Lossless methods permanently reduce the quality of the data
Compressed files need more storage space than the originals
q.why: Compression takes processing time (significant for video); only lossy methods lose quality.

q.q: A 36 000 000-byte photo is saved as a 3 000 000-byte JPEG. What is the compression ratio?
q.why: Compression ratio = original ÷ compressed = 36 000 000 ÷ 3 000 000 = 12 : 1.

q.q: A 36 000 000-byte photo is uploaded at 20 Mbps (20 000 000 bits per second). How long does the upload take?
o: 1.8 seconds
1.2 seconds
115.2 seconds
14.4 seconds
q.why: 36 000 000 bytes × 8 = 288 000 000 bits; ÷ 20 000 000 = 14.4 s. Forgetting to multiply by 8 gives 1.8 s.

q.q: Which statement about typical compression ratios matches the notes?
o: Text often compresses losslessly by about 10 : 1; JPEG photos often by about 2 : 1
Text often compresses losslessly by about 2 : 1; JPEG photos often by 10 : 1 or more
Text and JPEG photos both typically compress by about the same 2 : 1 ratio
Text cannot be compressed at all; JPEG photos often compress by 10 : 1 or more
q.why: Lossless text compression gives moderate savings; lossy JPEG gives much larger ones.

q.q: An uncompressed bitmap is 800 × 600 pixels in 24-bit colour. What is its size?
o: 1 440 000 bytes
480 000 bytes
1 920 000 bytes
q.why: 800 × 600 × 24 ÷ 8 = 1 440 000 bytes. Not dividing by 8 gives 11 520 000; using 8 bits per pixel gives 480 000.

q.q: A 4 × 5 inch photo is scanned at 150 dpi in 24-bit colour. What is the uncompressed size?
o: 450 000 bytes
1 350 000 bytes
9 000 bytes
q.why: Pixels = 600 × 750 = 450 000; × 3 bytes per pixel = 1 350 000 bytes. 450 000 forgets the colour depth.

q.q: A 3 × 2 inch picture is scanned at 200 dpi. How many pixels does the bitmap contain?
q.why: Width 3 × 200 = 600 px, height 2 × 200 = 400 px; 600 × 400 = 240 000 pixels. 1 200 multiplies by the dpi only once.

q.q: How many different colours can 24-bit colour depth represent?
q.why: 2^24 = 16 777 216 colours. 16 777 215 is the largest binary value, not the number of colours.

q.q: A photo is rescanned at 300 dpi instead of 150 dpi with the same colour depth. What happens to the bitmap size?
o: It becomes four times as large
It becomes twice as large
It stays the same
It becomes eight times as large
q.why: Doubling the dpi doubles both the width and the height in pixels, so the pixel count and size go up × 4.

q.q: The colour depth of a bitmap is reduced from 24 bits to 12 bits. What happens to its uncompressed size?
o: It falls to a quarter
It stays the same
It falls to one-twelfth
It halves
q.why: File size is directly proportional to colour depth, so halving the bits per pixel halves the size.

q.q: A mono sound is recorded at 8000 samples per second with 8-bit samples for 90 seconds. What is the uncompressed size?
o: 5 760 000 bytes
720 000 bytes
1 440 000 bytes
90 000 bytes
q.why: 8000 × 8 × 1 × 90 ÷ 8 = 720 000 bytes. 5 760 000 forgets to divide by 8; 1 440 000 assumes stereo.

q.q: Three minutes of CD-quality audio (44 100 samples/s, 16 bits, 2 channels) is recorded. What is the uncompressed size?
q.why: 44 100 × 16 × 2 × 180 ÷ 8 = 31 752 000 bytes. 254 016 000 is the size in bits; 10 584 000 is one minute.

q.q: A 31 752 000-byte WAV is saved as a 2 880 000-byte MP3. What is the approximate percentage saving?
o: About 91%
About 9%
About 11%
About 1100%
q.why: (31 752 000 − 2 880 000) ÷ 31 752 000 × 100 ≈ 91%. 9% is the size that remains, and 11 is the ratio.

q.q: A pupil calculates 1000 × 1400 × 24 = 33 600 000 and gives this as the bitmap's size in bytes. What is the error?
o: They should have divided by 24 rather than multiplied by it
They should have multiplied by 3 as well as by 24
They should have divided by 1024 to get the answer in bytes
They did not divide by 8 to convert bits into bytes
q.why: Width × height × colour depth gives bits; dividing by 8 gives 4 200 000 bytes.

q.q: Which file must be compressed losslessly?
o: A holiday photo for social media
An X-ray image used to make a diagnosis
A full-length film streamed to a smart TV
A music track stored on a phone
q.why: A changed pixel on an X-ray could affect a diagnosis, so the original must be restored exactly.

q.q: Which data does MP3 compression remove?
o: Every second sample, which halves the sample rate of the recording
Repeated sequences of bytes, which are replaced by dictionary tokens
Frequencies outside human hearing and quiet sounds masked by louder ones
Only the silence at the start and the end of the track
q.why: MP3 uses perceptual coding: it discards what listeners are unlikely to hear.

q.q: Why does JPEG compression reduce colour detail more than brightness detail?
o: The eye is more sensitive to changes in brightness than in colour
The eye is more sensitive to changes in colour than in brightness
Brightness data has already been compressed by the camera sensor
Colour needs 24 bits per pixel whereas brightness needs only 1 bit
q.why: Perceptual coding removes what the eye notices least, and it notices colour changes less than brightness changes.

q.q: How does MPEG video compression save space across frames?
o: Each frame is stored separately as a lossless image with its own palette
Much of each frame is predicted from neighbouring frames, so only the changes are stored
Every other frame is deleted, and each remaining frame is then shown twice during playback
Each frame is reduced to a 256-colour palette before it is stored
q.why: Storing only the changes between frames gives the huge saving that makes streaming practical.

q.q: Why do photo and video editors keep a lossless master copy?
o: Lossless files are smaller and quicker to edit
Lossy files cannot be opened by editing software
Lossless files stream without any buffering
Re-saving a lossy file loses more quality each time
q.why: Generation loss builds up with each lossy save, so editing is done from a lossless master.

q.q: A newspaper saved its website photos as lossy JPEGs. What would have been different with lossless compression?
o: Better quality and smaller files
Lower quality but smaller files
No loss of quality, but larger files
The same quality and the same file size
q.why: Lossless keeps every detail but gives a smaller reduction in size than lossy.

q.q: Which list contains only lossy formats?
o: ZIP, PNG, GIF, FLAC
JPEG, MP3, AAC, MPEG-4
JPEG, GIF, MP3, MPEG-4
JPEG, MP3, FLAC, MPEG-4
q.why: GIF and FLAC are lossless, so any list containing them is wrong.

q.q: What is the name for lossy compression that removes data human senses are unlikely to notice?
o: Perceptual coding
Run-length encoding
Dictionary-based coding
Redundancy removal
q.why: Perceptual coding relies on the limits of human sight and hearing; RLE and dictionary coding are lossless.

q.q: What is the run-length encoding of RRRRRGGBBBBBBB?
o: R5G2B7
5R2G6B
5R7B
5R2G7B
q.why: Five R, two G and seven B, each written as count then value.

q.q: Using count-then-value RLE, how is the 24-pixel row GGGGGGGGGGGGYYYYGGGGGGGG encoded?
o: 20G4Y
12G4Y8G
G12Y4G8
12G8Y4G
q.why: 12 green, 4 yellow, then 8 green. Runs are kept in order, so the two green runs cannot be combined.

q.q: Using simple count-then-value RLE, what does ABCD become?
o: ABCD, unchanged, because RLE leaves runs of one alone
4ABCD, with a single count for the whole string
A1B1C1D1, the same length, as each count simply replaces a letter
1A1B1C1D, twice as long, because each single value needs a count
q.why: With few repeats every value needs its own count, so RLE can double the size.

q.q: Which data would RLE compress best?
o: A scanned page with a large white background
A detailed photograph of a busy street at night
A file of random numbers
A paragraph of English text
q.why: RLE works well on long runs of identical values, such as white space, icons and cartoons.

q.q: Decode the RLE string 3A2B4A.
o: AAABBBBAA
AAAABBAAA
AAABBAAAA
ABABAAAA
q.why: Write A three times, B twice, then A four times.

q.q: In the C# RLE encoder, what is the purpose of the line i += count; at the end of the loop?
o: It adds the run length to the result string
It moves i to the first character of the next run
It counts how many characters are in the current run
It moves i on by exactly one character each time
q.why: After a run has been counted and written, i jumps past the whole run to start the next one.

q.q: In dictionary-based compression, how is each repeated word in the data represented?
o: By a short token that indexes its single entry in the dictionary
By a count of how many times the word appears in a row
By the number of letters that the word contains
It is deleted and reconstructed from context on decompression
q.why: Each word is stored once in the dictionary and every occurrence is replaced by a token pointing to it.

q.q: 'red lorry yellow lorry red lorry yellow lorry' (45 characters) is stored as a dictionary of red, lorry and yellow (14 characters) plus 8 one-byte tokens. What is the approximate compression ratio?
o: About 5.6 : 1
About 3.2 : 1
About 2 : 1
About 1 : 2
q.why: Compressed size ≈ 14 + 8 = 22 bytes; 45 ÷ 22 ≈ 2 : 1. 5.6 forgets the dictionary; 3.2 forgets the tokens.

q.q: Why might a very small file not shrink with dictionary-based compression?
o: Dictionary methods are lossy below a minimum size
Tokens are always longer than the words they replace
Small files contain no runs to be counted
The dictionary itself takes up space
q.why: With little repetition the saving is less than the space needed to store the dictionary.

q.q: A pupil writes 'GIF and RLE are both lossy'. What is the correct statement?
o: Both are lossless; the original can be restored exactly
GIF is lossless but RLE is lossy
RLE is lossless but GIF is lossy
Both are lossy, but only GIF loses colours when it is saved
q.why: Calling RLE or GIF lossy is a common error; both restore the data exactly.

q.q: Which type of compression does zipping use?
o: Lossy
Lossless
Perceptual coding
Lossy for images, lossless for text
q.why: Unzipping restores every file exactly, with its name and folder structure.

q.q: Which file would shrink the most when zipped?
o: An MP4 video of a concert
A JPEG photo of the team
A CSV file of pupil records
An existing ZIP archive
q.why: Text has many repeated words and characters; JPEG, MP4 and ZIP files are already compressed.

q.q: What happens when an existing ZIP file is zipped again?
o: It shrinks by about half again because DEFLATE is applied a second time
It loses some quality because zipping a file twice makes it lossy
It shrinks further because the archive headers are removed
There is no saving, and it may even grow slightly because of extra headers
q.why: Nothing is left to remove, and the new archive adds its own headers.

q.q: Which algorithm do zip programs use to compress files?
o: DEFLATE, which combines LZ77 with Huffman coding
Run-length encoding combined with perceptual coding
LZW combined with a 256-colour palette
MPEG frame prediction combined with LZ77
q.why: Zip uses the DEFLATE dictionary method (LZ77 plus Huffman coding).

q.q: Why can zipping be used on any type of file?
o: Every file is converted into plain text before compression
It discards whatever the user is unlikely to notice
The method works on the bytes, not on what they represent
It chooses a different lossy method for each file type
q.why: Zip looks for redundancy in the raw bytes, so it works on documents, images, sound and programs alike.

q.q: A designer must email a large BMP logo to a printer without any loss of quality. What should they do?
o: Save it as a heavily compressed JPEG to make it small
Zip the BMP so the printer can unzip an exact copy
Reduce its colour depth from 24 bits to 8 bits
Rescan it at a lower dpi so that the file is smaller
q.why: Zipping is lossless; the other options all permanently lose detail or colour.

q.q: Which is NOT a reason for zipping files?
o: To send several files as one email attachment
To archive old coursework using less storage
To download a whole project folder as one file
To improve the resolution of a photo
q.why: Zipping reduces size and bundles files; it cannot add detail to an image.

q.q: What does a plain text (.txt) file store?
o: Characters plus their fonts and bold styling, but no images
Characters plus images in a compressed form
An image of each page stored as a bitmap
Characters only, with no fonts, formatting or images
q.why: Plain text holds only characters (e.g. ASCII or UTF-8), which is why almost any program can open it.

q.q: One minute of CD-quality stereo WAV is 44 100 × 16 × 2 × 60 ÷ 8 bytes. About how large is this?
o: About 1 MB
About 80.7 MB
About 10.1 MB
About 5 MB
q.why: 10 584 000 bytes ≈ 10.1 MB. 80.7 MB is the result in bits; 5 MB would be mono.

q.q: Why is WAV a good format for a podcast's master recording?
o: It is lossy, so the file is small enough to publish
It is uncompressed, so no quality is lost while editing
It streams more efficiently than other audio formats
It keeps only the frequencies that people can hear
q.why: WAV keeps full quality for editing; it is then converted to MP3 to publish.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of using BMP images on a website?
o: The files are very large, so pages load slowly
Quality drops each time the file is saved
Only 256 colours can be stored per image
The images cannot be edited in a paint package
q.why: BMP stores every pixel uncompressed. Generation loss affects JPEG and the 256-colour limit applies to GIF.

q.q: What happens when a bitmap image is enlarged a great deal?
o: It becomes pixelated
It is recompressed with fewer colours
It is redrawn with sharper edges
Its colour depth automatically increases
q.why: A bitmap is a fixed grid of pixels, so enlarging it makes the individual pixels visible.

q.q: In a typical 24-bit BMP, how is each pixel's colour stored?
o: As an 8-bit index into a 256-colour palette
As 24 bits recording brightness only
As 3 bits each for red, green and blue
As 8 bits each for red, green and blue
q.why: 24 bits = 8 bits for each of the three primary colours. A palette index is how GIF stores pixels.

q.q: Which of these formats would gain the most from being zipped?
o: MP3
JPEG
WAV
MPEG-4
q.why: WAV is uncompressed, with lots of redundancy; the others are already compressed.

q.q: How does a GIF store each pixel?
o: As 24 bits, 8 each for red, green and blue
As an 8-bit index into a palette of up to 256 colours
As a lossy block shared with the neighbouring pixels
As a 16-bit index into a palette of 65 536 colours
q.why: Each 8-bit value points to a palette entry chosen from the full 24-bit range.

q.q: Why is GIF a poor choice for a detailed team photograph?
o: It is lossy, so detail is lost every time it is saved
It cannot be compressed, so the file is far too large
It can only store black-and-white images
It is limited to 256 colours, so the shading shows banding
q.why: Photographs need thousands of shades; GIF is lossless but limited to a 256-colour palette.

q.q: A 600 × 400 image is stored with an 8-bit palette. Ignoring the palette and compression, how large is the pixel data?
o: 720 000 bytes
1 920 000 bytes
240 000 bytes
768 bytes
q.why: 600 × 400 × 1 byte = 240 000 bytes, a third of the 720 000 bytes needed at 24-bit colour.

q.q: How many bytes does a full 256-colour palette need if each colour is stored in 24 bits?
q.why: 256 colours × 3 bytes = 768 bytes. 6144 is the size in bits.

q.q: Which format lets a photographer choose the balance between file size and visible quality?
o: GIF
JPEG
BMP
WAV
q.why: JPEG's compression level is adjustable: more compression gives a smaller file but more artefacts.

q.q: Why is JPEG a poor format for a logo with sharp edges and text?
o: It is limited to a palette of 256 colours, which causes banding
It is uncompressed, so the files are very large
Lossy compression creates blocky artefacts around the edges
It stores only one colour channel per pixel
q.why: JPEG suits continuous-tone photos; sharp edges and flat colours suit GIF or PNG.

q.q: Why is MPEG compression well suited to an on-demand service such as BBC iPlayer?
o: The slow encoding is done once, and the faster decoding happens for every viewer
Encoding is fast, so the video can be encoded again each time someone watches
It is lossless, so viewers see exactly the quality of the original recording
It needs no processing at all on the viewer's device to play the video
q.why: Encoding takes much more processing than decoding, so MPEG suits content written once and watched many times.

q.q: Which of these formats uses lossless compression?
o: JPEG
MP3
MPEG-4
GIF
q.why: GIF compresses palette indexes losslessly with LZW; the others are lossy.

q.q: Which is a drawback of MPEG video?
o: It cannot carry the audio together with the video
Quality loss, especially in fast motion at low bit rates
The files are left uncompressed, so they are too large to stream
It plays only on the device that encoded it
q.why: MPEG is lossy and slow to encode; MPEG-4 carries both video and audio and plays on almost any device.
